name: Udmurtia
summary_text: Udmurtia has produced no division-specific transgender evidence in the available sources. A visitor to the republic of Udmurtia stands under the national framework of Russia as it operates countrywide, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the framework against which this division is assessed.  Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the UK Home Office note records that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in November 2023.  The expanded 'propaganda' statute criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.  Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia, with 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reaching up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.  Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.  Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.  Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.  The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

name: Saint Helena
summary_text: The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the territory's own statutes and practices rather than the United Kingdom framework to determine how single-sex services, records and complaints are handled.  Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.  Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.  Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, and the applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is recorded on that basis.
